docs.abstract: A court in Beijing sentenced a man to six years in prison after finding him guilty of detonating a homemade bomb in Beijing’s Capital International Airport in July, state-run news media reported.
docs.snippet: A court in Beijing sentenced a man to six years in prison after finding him guilty of detonating a homemade bomb in Beijing’s Capital International Airport in July, state-run news media reported.
docs.lead_paragraph: A court in Beijing sentenced a man to six years in prison on Tuesday after finding him guilty of detonating a homemade bomb in Beijing’s Capital International Airport in July, state-run news media reported. The man, Ji Zhongxing, had been trying to draw attention to his allegations that officials in Dongguan, an industrial city in far southern China, ignored his complaints that security officers there beat him so severely in 2005 that he was unable to walk and had to use a wheelchair. The blast badly injured Mr. Ji and slightly wounded a police officer. The case kindled widespread debate in China, with some Internet users voicing sympathy for Mr. Ji and his ire with government officials. Dongguan officials said they had given him compensation of 100,000 renminbi, or about $16,400, on condition that he drop his complaints. Mr. Ji pleaded not guilty to the charges. His lawyers argued that he had not meant to detonate the explosive, the China News Service reported. The maximum sentence for the charge was 10 years in prison.

headline.main: China: 6-Year Term for Protester in Blast

That’s not 1% off GDP — it’s the annualized rate of growth, so that we’re talking about almost 3% of GDP at this point; cumulatively, the losses come to around $700 billion of wasted economic potential. This is in the same ballpark as my own estimates.

docs.abstract: The ones who will really get hit by all the cans we’re kicking down the road are young people. Are they paying attention?
docs.snippet: The ones who will really get hit by all the cans we’re kicking down the road are young people. Are they paying attention?
docs.lead_paragraph: Eventually this shutdown crisis will end. And eventually the two parties will make another stab at a deal on taxes, investments and entitlements. But there’s one outcome from such negotiations that I can absolutely guarantee: Seniors, Wall Street and unions will all have their say and their interests protected. So the most likely result will be more tinkering around the edges, as our politicians run for the hills the minute someone accuses them of “fixing the deficit on the backs of the elderly” or creating “death panels” to sensibly allocate end-of-life health care. Could this time be different? Short of an economic meltdown, there is only one thing that might produce meaningful change: a mass movement for tax, spending and entitlement reform led by the cohort that is the least organized but will be the most affected if we don’t think long term — today’s young people.

headline.main: Sorry, Kids. We Ate It All.

docs.lead_paragraph: For most of us, Lee Harvey Oswald exists most vividly in downtown Dallas, poised to make the worst kind of history. In his new book, “The Interloper,” Peter Savodnik recounts Oswald’s time living and working in the Soviet Union. He went in 1960, with the hopes of building a permanent existence there after a childhood of frequent moves. He found his future wife, and became a father for the first time, but he returned to the United States in 1962, bitterly disappointed in his failure to start over in Russia. Mr. Savodnik argues that this time overseas reveals a great deal about Oswald’s personality and his infamous crime. In a recent e-mail interview, Mr. Savodnik discussed Oswald’s time in Minsk, the Russian view of conspiracy theories and more. Below are edited excerpts from the conversation:

docs.snippet: Beginning tomorrow in Los Angeles, John Knuth will exhibit process-based pieces derived from light bulbs, melted sugar and smoke that rely on gravitational pull for their shape.
docs.lead_paragraph: John Knuth comes from a school of artists who allow nature to activate their works. But unlike some who let their pieces be entirely dictated by the whims of the elements, the Los Angeles-based artist remains involved with the process, exerting a measure of control over his science-based abstractions. His recent series of fly paintings — in which he fed the insects pigment, which they then regurgitated onto canvases — were ironically beautiful gradients of pointillist abstraction. For his next body of work, which he will create on site at Human Resources, an art space in Los Angeles’s Chinatown, the process is even messier.

headline.main: An Artist Who Gets a Lift From Gravity

docs.lead_paragraph: Nili Lotan, whose namesake line of luxe basics is a wardrobe staple for both celebrities and everyday, on-the-go women, introduced her spring 2014 collection last Thursday with a performance in her TriBeCa showroom. The Israeli-American designer said that the “very minimal, clean, pure” aesthetic of her 25 new pieces remained true to the vision of her very first collection a decade ago. To present the clothes, she commissioned LeeSaar the Company to incorporate them into an original modern dance, but because the spring looks weren’t designed specifically for dancers, she faced a few obstacles in preparing for the unusual show format. “It’s not models, so you’re not dealing with size 2,” she said. “They’re short and they’re big-muscled, and it was a challenge because most of the samples are a size 2, size 4.” She wound up designing special briefs for the dancers to perform in.

Bolden released Ms. Tsarnaeva, who now lives in New Jersey, on $1,500 personal recognizance and required her to check in weekly with probation officers. docs.abstract: Why the shutdown fiasco was more a failure of followership than leadership.
docs.snippet: Why the shutdown fiasco was more a failure of followership than leadership.
docs.lead_paragraph: As a follow-up to my post on the lessons of the shutdown, and my insistence on the essentially indefensible folly of what we’ve just witnessed from House Republicans, let me say something about the alternative interpretation that’s come up in a number of mini-debates I’ve had on Twitter over the last week or so, with conservative writers like the Weekly Standard’s Jay Cost and Sean Davis of the nascent webzine The Federalist. Against my indictment of the Republican caucus as a whole, they’ve basically argued that the seeming irrationality of G.O.P. strategy across the last few weeks mostly just reflects the mistakes, shading into incompetence, of John Boehner’s negotiating strategy, rather the kind of deeper, essentially methodless dysfunction that I see when I look at the House Republicans. At bottom, these interlocutors think that the House Republicans are a fairly normal majority with a serious leadership problem, and they think I’m a victim of what you might call the pundit’s limited-horizon problem, which fails to work in vitally-useful knowledge — political science research in Cost’s case, business-school theory in Davis’s case — that would pin more of the responsibility on Boehner, and less on his backbenchers. (You can also read a more personalized version of this argument here, from the pseudonymous blogger Thomas Crown, which is based on a slight misreading of a tweet I wrote to Davis — such are the perils of Twitter! — but which works off the entirely correct assumption that my analysis of internal House dynamics lacks the benefit of sustained personal experience with high-stakes negotiations in politics, law or the business world.)

headline.main: Was It All Boehner’s Fault?

Now she’s back, as they like to say in movie ads, in a fine, largely faithful screen remake, directed by Kimberly Peirce that stars Chloë Grace Moretz as its goddess of gore. docs.snippet: Claudia Roth Pierpont’s look at Philip Roth’s career is a critical biography of the old school.
docs.lead_paragraph: American anti-Semitism, which was running high throughout the 1930s, steadily increased after the onset of war. During the entire period, polls showed, well over a third of the populace stood ready to back discriminatory laws. Nor was this a mere offshoot of the general xenophobia spawned by isolationism. Every synagogue in Washington Heights was desecrated (and some were smeared with swastikas); in Boston, beatings, wreckings and defilements had become near-daily occurrences by 1942. The disgraceful fever, which ruled out all but a trickle of immigration and so cost countless lives, reached its historic apogee in 1944 — by which time the Holocaust was more or less complete.

headline.main: His Subject, Himself

docs.abstract: J. Michael Lennon’s full-scale biography of Norman Mailer does not sand the corners of a career and life with plenty of texture and lots of sharp edges.
docs.snippet: J. Michael Lennon’s full-scale biography of Norman Mailer does not sand the corners of a career and life with plenty of texture and lots of sharp edges.
docs.lead_paragraph: It could be said that Norman Mailer was a man and a writer halfway between fame and infamy and yet with little in the way of middle ground. He was, in varying combinations, a world-class drinker, feuder, provocateur, self-mythologizer and anti-feminist. He was a war protester, a mayoral candidate, a co-founder of The Village Voice, as well as a wife stabber, a serial husband (of six wives), and a father (of nine). He was a boxer, an actor, a filmmaker, a poet and a playwright. He was also a journalist and a novelist of enormous and singular narrative inventiveness and thrust, a two-time Pulitzer Prize winner, and one of the least boring and most tireless and tiresome public figures of the last half of the 20th century.

headline.main: Fame and Infamy
headline.print_headline: Towering Figures: 'Norman Mailer'

docs.abstract: Clare Vivier opens her first East Coast outpost in NoLIta today, where her West Coast-made leather goods are sure to be a hit with East Coast girls.
docs.snippet: Clare Vivier opens her first East Coast outpost in NoLIta today, where her West Coast-made leather goods are sure to be a hit with East Coast girls.
docs.lead_paragraph: The leather goods designer and retailer Clare Vivier is one of the most prominent ambassadors of the new Los Angeles fashion scene. Yet her bags are especially well suited to the demands of life in New York. The line, recently rebranded as Clare V., is polished enough for a party, but not too precious for the subway — auxiliary pouches and pockets cleverly accommodate gadgets or spare pairs of shoes. “New York is full of working women who want to look chic while being prepared for all sorts of situations,” Vivier said. Those women can now find the entire Clare V. range at the brand’s second boutique and first East Coast outpost, which opens tonight in a former dressmaker’s shop on Elizabeth Street in NoLIta. Walking into the space feels like being transported to California, thanks to its airy, light-flooded interior (by the L.A.-based architect Barbara Bestor, who also designed Vivier’s Silver Lake flagship) and its mostly SoCal-sourced lifestyle goods (jewelry by Annie Costello Brown, hats by Westbrook Maker, scented candles from the Chateau Marmont). Monograms, a Vivier signature, can be embossed on the spot. Also on view, and worth a visit in its own right, is a colorful nine-foot-wide collage wall by the New York florist and artist Simone Shubuck, a close friend of Vivier’s for 20 years.

headline.main: In Store | L.A.-Made Handbags That Feel Right at Home in New York

docs.snippet: A playful jewelry line by the Greek designer Elena Votsi, which includes a gold ring shaped like a baby rattle and a sinuous swirl of rhythm, comes to Bergdorf Goodman beginning today.
docs.lead_paragraph: Beginning today, a 10-piece collection of jewelry by the Greek designer Elena Votsi, who has stores in Athens and Hydra (where the pieces are made), will be available for the first time stateside at Bergdorf Goodman on Fifth Avenue. In the short film above, “A Day in Hydra with Elena Votsi,” the artisan, who designed the medal for the 2004 Olympic Games in Athens, discusses her own history and design inspiration for the rings, necklaces and earrings that she likens to objects, like “toys,” that can be as fun alone as they are on the body. It’s no wonder, then, that included among her selection of work at Bergdorf Goodman is a gold ball ring that resembles a baby’s rattle and a gold-and-diamond ring that looks like a wound-up ribbon, which in Greek culture is a symbol for everything from athletics to marriage. “Even from a very young age I loved Greek history,” said Votsi, who discusses her Hydra roots in the video, which was produced by LoveGold, an online community dedicated to gold jewelry.

headline.main: A New Line | Whimsical Objects, Imported From the Island of Hydra Straight to Fifth Avenue

docs.snippet: In “Lost for Words,” a lonely American man meets a wistful Chinese woman before coming face to face with oppression.
docs.lead_paragraph: The conventions are trundled out in Stanley J. Orzel’s cross-cultural romance, “Lost for Words,” but not the tension or the chemistry. Sean Faris, resembling a very poor man’s Ethan Hawke, plays Michael Vance, a former Marine who has been hired by the information technology department of a company in Hong Kong. Michael is despondent, having been dumped by his girlfriend stateside, until he meets a dancer, Anna Zhou (the gorgeous if opaque Grace Huang, assaying a woefully underdrawn character). How do they meet? He bumps into her as he arrives at the airport and as he jogs in a park.

headline.main: An American Adrift in Hong Kong

docs.abstract: Chad, Chile, Lithuania, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia were elected Thursday to seats on the 15-member United Nations Security Council for two-year terms starting in January.
docs.snippet: Chad, Chile, Lithuania, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia were elected Thursday to seats on the 15-member United Nations Security Council for two-year terms starting in January.
docs.lead_paragraph: Chad, Chile, Lithuania, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia were elected Thursday to seats on the 15-member United Nations Security Council for two-year terms starting in January. It was the first time that Saudi Arabia had sought to gain one of the nonpermanent seats on the Council; its decision to vie for a seat appeared to reflect the kingdom’s wish to be more assertive in resolving the Syria war and the Arab-Israeli conflict. The Saudis, who support the rebellion seeking the ouster of President Bashar al-Assad of Syria, have criticized the Council over what they regard as its insufficient response to the turmoil in the Middle East. Last month the Saudi foreign minister canceled his General Assembly speech, apparently to show the Saudis’ displeasure. The new Council members replace Azerbaijan, Guatemala, Morocco, Pakistan and Togo.

headline.main: Security Council Elects 5 New Members

docs.lead_paragraph: Israeli soldiers on Thursday fatally shot a Palestinian man who drove a construction vehicle into an army base near Ramallah in the West Bank, barging through a gate and repeatedly trying to run over a soldier, the Israeli military said in a statement. The official Palestinian news agency Wafa identified the man as Yunis Radeideh, 30. In two attacks in July 2008, Palestinians driving construction vehicles in central Jerusalem were shot and killed after plowing into traffic and pedestrians, killing three Israelis. In March 2009, the Palestinian driver of an earthmover flipped over an Israeli police car, wounding two police officers before he was shot dead. According to initial reports, the driver in that episode, Marei al-Radeideh, was a brother of the driver killed at the army base on Thursday.

docs.lead_paragraph: The first and possibly last amusing thing about Hookworms, a band from Leeds, is its name. Hooks and catchiness (ohrwurm, which translates to “earworm,” is a German term for an all-too-catchy song) are extremely low priorities for a band that is built around Minimalist repetition, kinetic drones and an onslaught of guitars and keyboards. They do play what could loosely be called rock songs; Matt Johnson, the keyboardist, sometimes shrieks phrases that are probably English words, though they go through so much reverb and echo there’s rarely a chance of deciphering them. But Hookworms also spent part of their set, and their debut album “Pearl Mystic,” creating and sustaining noises that are deliberately amorphous: no beat, just resonance and distortion.

docs.lead_paragraph: Having endured a summer of existential threats to the planet — zombie hordes, alien invaders, the usual stuff — moviegoers can now settle in for an autumn of more intimately scaled ordeals. Spectacles of collective apocalypse, the staple of the blockbuster economy, give way to individual stories of adversity and the struggle to survive in limited space. Superheroes step aside in favor of ordinary (albeit highly competent) people equipped with nerve, resourcefulness and impressive but not always reliable technology. Their archenemies are the laws of nature and political economy, abstract forces that take the form of lethal satellite debris, heavy weather and desperate pirates.

docs.snippet: Claire Denis may be a fearless filmmaker, but she is preoccupied with making films about family with the help of a surrogate family of collaborators.
docs.lead_paragraph: Some people are troubled by contradictions — by impulses clashing with intentions, needs complicating wants, violence coexisting with compassion. The director Claire Denis thrives on such things. From her autobiographical debut in 1989, “Chocolat,” to modernist reveries like “Beau Travail” (1999) and “The Intruder” (2004), she has searched for sublimity in the profane and exploited the terror in ecstasy. And while she may be the most independent filmmaker in France, she is preoccupied with belonging, making films about family with the help of a surrogate family of collaborators.

docs.lead_paragraph: While designing the kitchen at his namesake restaurant on Columbus Circle, Jean-Georges Vongerichten traded American efficiency for Old World tyranny. The five food stations, staffed by six cooks (two on fish) and one floating chef (a chef de tournant) are arranged perpendicular to the pass, which is where the food is handed off to the food runners (seen at the bottom of the page), all under the scrutiny of another chef, who runs the line. Typically, Vongerichten says, “you cook against the wall, turn around, plate it and it goes out.” At Jean-Georges, the staff members cook various elements at their stations and then walk them up to the pass — where they assemble the dishes with monastic precision. When your shrimp appetizer, being plated lower left by two cooks, comes with crispy baby artichokes, crispy mushrooms, smoked paprika gel, lemon fennel purée, microthyme and parsley, a more collaborative and focused effort is required. (Also: tweezers).

docs.lead_paragraph: For much of the last 35 years, the wine critic Robert Parker dominated the international wine scene. Parker invented the 100-point rating system for wine, and his reviews wielded such influence over sales that vintners everywhere worked to please Parker’s palate, making oaky, intensely flavored, high-alcohol wines. Kermit Lynch, meanwhile, through his wine shop in Berkeley, Calif., and also through his nationwide distribution business, chose to sell only French and Italian wines made in the unadulterated, old-school traditional style aimed at accentuating terroir — each vineyard’s unique combination of weather, soil and geography.

docs.snippet: How the passion of Chowhound’s amateur critics can define a city’s cuisine.
docs.lead_paragraph: Everyone with Internet access is a critic, but some forms of amateur criticism have higher standing than others. Amateur literary critics, like Dylan Lucia, an Amazon reviewer who gave one star to “Fahrenheit 451” (“Bradbury is a good writer [I’ll give him that], but I HATE his writing style”), may lack a nuanced understanding of the English language; some amateur film critics, like the IMDB reviewer who gave 10 stars to “Wrath of the Titans” (“i never saw a movie this good before in my life”), may have never seen another movie before in their lives. But all of us with a tongue and a functioning digestive tract are authorities on food. After all, we have a commanding range of experience to draw from: we eat, according to one study, an average of 4.9 times a day. When it comes to food, everyone is not just a critic — everyone is a connoisseur.

docs.lead_paragraph: Scientists disagree about when humans first tasted kale. But it is known that the ancient Greeks cultivated leafy greens, which they boiled and ate as a cure for drunkenness. And early Roman manuscripts include references to “brassica,” a word that encompassed wild turnips, cabbages and kalelike plants. By the Middle Ages, kale had spread through Europe and Asia. The Italians developed plants with “dinosaur” scales, while the Scots created varietals with leaves like frilly petticoats. The Russians produced kale that could survive in the snow. But by the time Tim Peters, who was then farming in Oregon, began experimenting with the plant in the 1980s, kale had become “boring.” “You only saw the green kind in the supermarket,” he says, “if you could find it at all.”

docs.snippet: Bill O’Reilly and Jesse (the Body) Ventura both have best-sellers about the Kennedy assassination, and the former wrestler has challenged the TV host to a debate.
docs.lead_paragraph: 11/22/63: As the 50th anniversary of the Kennedy assassination approaches, Americans remain divided on the big question: Who did it? According to an Associated Press-GfK poll conducted in April, 59 percent of the country believes in a conspiracy, while 24 percent accepts the Warren Commission’s conclusion that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone. Another 16 percent isn’t sure. (Yes, that adds up to 99 percent. The rest probably blames President Obama.) The best-seller list reflects this split personality. “Killing Kennedy,” by Bill O’Reilly and Martin Dugard, echoes the Warren Report’s lone gunman thesis and has spent 34 weeks on the hardcover nonfiction list; it’s currently on the extended list at No. 22. Meanwhile, a new case for conspiracy hits the nonfiction ­list at No. 14: “They Killed Our President,” by the renowned historian and investigative journalist Jesse (the Body) Ventura, who with Dick Russell and David Wayne argues the president was killed by “disgruntled C.I.A. agents, anti-Castro Cubans and members of the Mafia. . . . Members of the U.S. military were also involved.” Like the former professional wrestler he is, Ventura confronts his biggest rival head on. “Since Bill O’Reilly apparently thinks he knows so much about the J.F.K. assassination,” he writes, “I’d like to publicly challenge him. . . . How about a public debate? Let’s do it. Let’s set it up! I’ll be there, Bill.”

docs.abstract: In his latest thriller, “The October List,” Jeffery Deaver begins the story with Chapter 36 and methodically works his way back to Chapter 1.
docs.snippet: In his latest thriller, “The October List,” Jeffery Deaver begins the story with Chapter 36 and methodically works his way back to Chapter 1.
docs.lead_paragraph: The temptation to read THE OCTOBER LIST (Grand Central, $26) backward — which is to say, forward — must be resisted, or you’ll hate yourself for spoiling what might well be Jeffery Deaver’s most fiendish thriller ever. Taking inspiration from Kierke­gaard (“Life can only be understood backward; but it must be lived forward”), the devious author begins his story with Chapter 36 and methodically works his way back to Chapter 1. Let’s admit that the prose is a bit flat, and the characters lack nuance, the unavoidable consequence of withholding key information about persons and motives until those last (first!) five chapters give it all up. The reader is never lied to in Deaver’s brilliant shell game, merely misdirected, and the best part of this trick is that despite being in on the game, we continue to make false assumptions.

docs.lead_paragraph: On Feb. 24, 2010, Dawn Brancheau, a senior trainer at SeaWorld Orlando in Florida, was killed when Tilikum, a 12,000-pound bull orca, grabbed her as they interacted in shallow water and dragged her into a deep pool, mutilating and drowning her. It was the third human death the whale had been implicated in since 1991. “If you were in a bathtub for 25 years, don’t you think you’d get a little irritated, aggravated, maybe a little psychotic?” Jane Velez-Mitchell suggested afterward in a CNN panel discussion. But had Tilikum turned violent from the stress of living outside his natural environment? Or was he, like the overgrown kid he was portrayed as, just playing?

docs.lead_paragraph: After playing seven years in his 14-year professional soccer career for his hometown team, Mike Petke believes he can lead the Red Bulls to the promised land — a championship in Major League Soccer. The club, first as the MetroStars and later as an outpost in the energy drink empire of an Austrian company, have gone to the league’s title match once — in 2008, losing by 3-1 to Columbus. After two years as an assistant to Hans Backe, Petke was named the team’s interim coach, then got the job full-time only weeks before the start of the 2013 season. The first team to clinch a playoff berth, if the Red Bulls win their final two regular-season games (at Houston on Sunday and against Chicago on Oct. 27) they will finish No. 1 over all, win the Supporters Shield and a berth in next season’s Concacaf Champions League. Petke spoke with Jack Bell of The Times before training on Tuesday at the Red Bulls training complex in Hanover, N.J.

But, in the last few weeks, I’ve felt myself to be at a real advantage trying to explain American politics. You see, it turns out that all those years covering Sunnis and Shiites, Israelis and Palestinians, tribal conflicts and “Parties of God” have been the best preparation for covering today’s Washington, D.C., and particularly the Tea Party. docs.abstract: In our latest issue, we explore distinct forms of design, from fashion, furniture and architecture.
docs.snippet: In our latest issue, we explore distinct forms of design, from fashion, furniture and architecture.
docs.lead_paragraph: In our latest issue, we explore distinct forms of design, whether they’re found in the asymmetrical forms of fashion, or in the ’70s-style curvilinear lines of furniture, or in the architecture of midcentury homes in the Beverly Hills neighborhood of Trousdale. Design, like all forms of art, can be very personal; members of one of England’s most celebrated families, Emma, Issy and Stella Tennant, draw inspiration from nature, namely from the bucolic surroundings in Scotland to create their sculptures and paintings. It can also be very pared down and minimal, like in the home of two fashion designers in Tokyo, or in the distilled, spacious Antwerp residence of the Belgian architect Vincent Van Duysen. On a larger scale, we discover designers and artisans determined to reinvent neighborhoods and cities around the world. In Sydney’s Rosebery neighborhood, three businesses celebrate the best of the city’s agriculture, craftsmanship and furniture design. Meanwhile, in Belgrade, locals are turning their city into a world-class destination, with the emergence of design hotels, art museums and adventurous restaurants. We embrace those who break with convention in art and design; Not Vital, a Swiss artist obsessed with habitats, is the Picasso, the Dali, the Andy Warhol of today, claims Andrew O’Hagan. Howard Slatkin’s Fifth Avenue apartment is filled with custom-made items, from floor to ceiling; each room has a combination of textiles, lighting, objets d’art from different eras and countries. Last but not least, we celebrate visionaries who are using technology to take design — and our imaginations — to the next level. See all stories from the issue >>

headline.main: T Fall Design Issue

docs.lead_paragraph: 8 P.M. (HBO) MAMA (2013) In this modern fairy tale directed by Andy Muschietti, the uncle (Nikolaj Coster-Waldau) of two feral sisters (Megan Charpentier, above, and Isabelle Nélisse), abandoned by their father in the woods, moves them into a home with his Goth girlfriend (Jessica Chastain). Then a grotesque figure the girls call Mama appears in the shadows and begins to wreak havoc on their lives. But is the monster simply a coping mechanism for dealing with tragedy? Or is Mama the essence of the girls’ dead mother? “Instead of delivering buckets of guts and gore, this ghost story offers a strong sense of time and place, along with the kind of niceties that don’t often figure into horror flicks, notably pictorial beauty, an atmosphere throbbing with dread and actors so good that you don’t want anyone to take an ax to them,” Manohla Dargis wrote in The New York Times. And while the director, Guillermo del Toro, “the reigning godfather of motion picture horror,” took only an executive producing credit on the film, “it fits with the more successful movies he’s signed onto. Mr. del Toro understands that nothing says terror like a home that’s become a rattling cage.”

docs.abstract: The case for libraries.
docs.snippet: The case for libraries.
docs.lead_paragraph: The coolest library I’ve ever been to is in a book. It’s a literal labyrinth, made that way to scare off medieval monks from pursuing forbidden knowledge. There are 50-some seven-sided rooms and a few more square ones, and all of them have varying numbers of doors to the other rooms, and each is named after a Latin verse from the Apocalypse of John. Additional features include distorting mirrors, psychotropic herbs to induce visions and a ventilation system that whistles and feels like ghosts breathing on your face.

docs.lead_paragraph: In early September 1863, a young Union soldier wrote a letter to his former professor back at Oberlin College, where he had studied before the war. The soldier, who identified himself only as “G,” had been tasked with taking a census of the freedmen on Craney Island, near Norfolk, Va. The African-American population of the area had been swelling since the arrival of Union forces the previous May, and soldiers like G were to provide the first step toward, among other things, organizing and recruiting black soldiers for the war effort.

These cards, issued by specialty finance companies as well as commercial banks, carry exorbitant interest rates after an initial period of zero interest expires — with heavy penalties for late payments. They are often pushed on patients with modest incomes by health care providers who want to make sure that they get paid, even if some of their patients end up with huge credit card bills they can’t afford. Unless strong regulatory action is taken to curb the abuses, financial companies will continue to gouge consumers at their most vulnerable moments, when they are in pain and need medical attention.

docs.abstract: Readers comment on my column suggesting that poultry are smarter and more sophisticated than we give them credit for.
docs.snippet: Readers comment on my column suggesting that poultry are smarter and more sophisticated than we give them credit for.
docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column looks at the ethical reasons to be wary of eating chicken, geese and other poultry produced in factory farms. My colleague Mark Bittman had an excellent column a few days ago about the health reasons to be wary, and in particular the salmonella risk. I agree with everything Mark said but want to go a step further. Even aside from the health issues, I think there are particular issues with the way poultry are raised, jammed in pens. Part of that is economics: it’s cheap to raise hens in cages, while cows and calves typically get pasture because that’s cheaper. And part of it is, I think, that we have some natural sympathy and regard for fellow mammals like cattle or hogs, but we dismiss birds as lower animals less deserving of our moral concern.

headline.main: Hold the Drumstick! That’s an Intellectual You’re Eating!

docs.abstract: Conservatives often present Robert Nozick’s view that an unfettered free market leads to a just society as moral common sense. But is it?
docs.snippet: Conservatives often present Robert Nozick’s view that an unfettered free market leads to a just society as moral common sense. But is it?
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1971 John Rawls published “A Theory of Justice,” the most significant articulation and defense of political liberalism of the 20th century. Rawls proposed that the structure of a just society was the one that a group of rational actors would come up with if they were operating behind a “veil of ignorance” — that is, provided they had no prior knowledge what their gender, age, wealth, talents, ethnicity and education would be in the imagined society. Since no one would know in advance where in society they would end up, rational agents would select a society in which everyone was guaranteed basic rights, including equality of opportunity. Since genuine (rather than “on paper”) equality of opportunity requires substantial access to resources — shelter, medical care, education — Rawls’s rational actors would also make their society a redistributive one, ensuring a decent standard of life for everyone.

headline.main: Questions for Free-Market Moralists

(HBO) LIFE ACCORDING TO SAM (2013) In 1998, Dr. Leslie Gordon and Dr. Scott Berns discovered that their 2-year-old son, Sam, above, had progeria, a rare and untreatable progressive aging disorder that leads the children afflicted with it — at the time, fewer than 250 in the world — eventually to die of a heart attack or stroke at an average age of 13. But the couple weren’t about to give up on finding a cure, or empowering their son to enjoy life. Sam is now 17, a high school junior and an avid sports fan who excels at his studies, music and friendships. “I didn’t put myself in front of you to have you feel bad for me,” Sam says at the beginning of this documentary, directed by Sean Fine and Andrea Nix Fine. “I put myself in front of you to let you know you don’t need to feel bad for me.” His mother responds: “You are handed something, and what you do with it is what matters, and that’s what Sam is doing. docs.abstract: The new Broadway double bill of Shakespeare’s “Twelfth Night” and “Richard III,” running in repertory, had a solid first week of ticket sales.
docs.snippet: The new Broadway double bill of Shakespeare’s “Twelfth Night” and “Richard III,” running in repertory, had a solid first week of ticket sales.
docs.lead_paragraph: The new Broadway double bill of Shakespeare’s “Twelfth Night” and “Richard III,” running in repertory and starring the two-time Tony Award winner Mark Rylance as Olivia and Richard, had a solid first week of ticket sales, according to data released on Monday by the Broadway League, a trade association of theater owners and producers. The shows grossed $468,429 for a total of six preview performances — 73 percent of the maximum possible amount, a high level of plays. The gross is notable partly because the shows are setting aside 250 tickets at every performance for an unusually low $25, which would theoretically lower the amount of money in ticket sales somewhat. The new musical “After Midnight,” a revue recreating the Cotton Club nightclub scene, also had a good first week, grossing $235,823 for three previews (or 64 percent of the maximum possible amount). Over all, Broadway musicals and plays grossed $24 million last week, compared to $24.6 million the previous week, which fell over the Columbus Day holiday weekend. Attendance at shows totaled 233,682 last week, compared to 232,400 the previous week.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Brazilian authorities on Monday awarded a license to develop oil production in a coveted deep-sea area to a consortium of five companies: Petrobras, Brazil’s national oil company; the Western oil giants Shell and Total; and two Chinese state-controlled oil companies. The group, the only consortium to submit a bid in the auction, will pay a signing fee of about $7 billion to start work on the 35-year concession. The deep-sea field, called Libra, is believed to be one of Brazil’s most promising exploration areas. Legislation requires the Brazilian company to take control of the new operation, but doubts persist among energy analysts as to whether Petrobras, which has soaring debt and is trying to reverse a decline in Brazil’s oil production, is overstretched with an array of offshore projects. The auction was carried out in Rio de Janeiro amid protests by oil workers and other groups that oppose the participation of foreign companies in Brazil’s oil industry.

headline.main: Brazil: Consortium Wins Oil Rights

docs.abstract: How Lincoln and the Union Army finally brought Maryland’s Southern sympathizers to heel.
docs.snippet: How Lincoln and the Union Army finally brought Maryland’s Southern sympathizers to heel.
docs.lead_paragraph: On Oct. 21, 1863, an indignant delegation of slaveholders from St. Mary’s County, Md., on the western shore of Chesapeake Bay just across the Potomac River from Virginia, confronted President Abraham Lincoln at the White House. They demanded that he suspend recruiting efforts aimed at their slaves. The presence of “armed colored troops” was “frightening quiet people, and producing great confusion,” they told him. Lincoln listened sympathetically to the grievances voiced by these alleged Union supporters; he did not, he told them, want the Army behaving in “any rude or ungentlemanly manner.”

headline.main: Holding the Line in Maryland

docs.abstract: Federal workers hit by the shutdown will be counted as employed in one Labor Department survey and unemployed in another, meaning a possible impact on the jobless rate but not the job growth figure.
docs.snippet: Federal workers hit by the shutdown will be counted as employed in one Labor Department survey and unemployed in another, meaning a possible impact on the jobless rate but not the job growth figure.
docs.lead_paragraph: There has been a lot of speculation about how the federal government shutdown will affect numbers for the October jobs report, due out Nov. 8. The jobs report is based on two different surveys — one of households, and one of employers — and it turns out that furloughed federal government workers will be treated as unemployed in the first survey but employed in the second. In other words, the temporary layoff of federal workers will probably increase the unemployment rate, but not (at least directly) depress the payroll job growth numbers.

headline.main: How the Furloughed Will Be Counted
headline.print_headline: How To Count Furloughs

docs.abstract: Getting down to bedrock in the great health care debate.
docs.snippet: Getting down to bedrock in the great health care debate.
docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column on the potential consequences of Obamacare’s botched rollout ended by sketching a scenario in which the program’s Medicaid expansion is deemed a success while its reform of the individual market leads to much-higher-than-expected costs and much-lower-than-expected participation rates. This combination would no doubt be politically helpful to the Republican Party in the short run, but (I argued) it would actually leave liberals with a fairly clear path forward: Keep pressing the Medicaid expansion on states that haven’t taken it (and look for John Kasich-style Republicans to partner with), return to the Joe Lieberman-killed idea of expanding Medicare to 55-and-overs, and basically try to further shrink the percentage of Americans who aren’t eligible for one or both of those single-payer programs. This wouldn’t amount to the full-on push for single payer that some people expect from the left if Obamacare fails or gets repealed, but it would move the U.S. toward the closest thing to single payer that we’re ever likely to get: A system in which both the late middle-aged and the lower middle class gradually get folded into government-run insurance alongside the poor, the disabled, and the aged; the individual market survives as a kind of de facto high risk pool (overpriced but technically accessible); and the employer mandate helps prop up employer-based health insurance for a shrunken but still substantial share of the population.

headline.main: Why Not Medicaid For All?

docs.abstract: A Moscow court opened and then rescheduled the first public hearing in the case of an acid attack against the artistic director of the Bolshoi Theater.
docs.snippet: A Moscow court opened and then rescheduled the first public hearing in the case of an acid attack against the artistic director of the Bolshoi Theater.
docs.lead_paragraph: A Moscow court on Tuesday opened and then quickly rescheduled the first public hearing in the case of an acid attack against the artistic director of the Bolshoi Theater, which seems set to look into personal grievances in one of the world’s premier ballet troupes. Pavel Dmitrichenko, above, the former principal dancer accused of paying two co-defendants to ambush the artistic director, Sergei Filin, with a mixture of sulfuric acid and urine in January, entered the courtroom in handcuffs and wore a slight smile as he stated his name and place of birth before the judge. Prosecutors were expected to read charges against Mr. Dmitrichenko on Tuesday but the case was rescheduled to next week because a lawyer for another of the accused did not attend the hearing. While the Bolshoi had been known for its atmosphere of extreme, and sometimes destructive, competition, the acid attack sent shock waves through Russia’s theater community and further exposed animosities among some of the troupe’s most gifted dancers.

headline.main: Hearing Starts for Dancer Accused in Bolshoi Attack

docs.abstract: How these schools in China made it to No. 1 in the world.
docs.snippet: How these schools in China made it to No. 1 in the world.
docs.lead_paragraph: SHANGHAI — Whenever I visit China, I am struck by the sharply divergent predictions of its future one hears. Lately, a number of global investors have been “shorting” China, betting that someday soon its powerful economic engine will sputter, as the real estate boom here turns to a bust. Frankly, if I were shorting China today, it would not be because of the real estate bubble, but because of the pollution bubble that is increasingly enveloping some of its biggest cities. Optimists take another view: that, buckle in, China is just getting started, and that what we’re now about to see is the payoff from China’s 30 years of investment in infrastructure and education. I’m not a gambler, so I’ll just watch this from the sidelines. But if you’re looking for evidence as to why the optimistic bet isn’t totally crazy, you might want to visit a Shanghai elementary school.

headline.main: The Shanghai Secret

docs.lead_paragraph: The National Security Agency wiretapped the offices of the French mission to the United Nations and the French Embassy in Washington, according to an article published Tuesday in the French newspaper Le Monde. The disclosure, as well as similar material published in the German magazine Der Spiegel in September, was based on secret documents provided by Edward J. Snowden, a former N.S.A. contractor. Both reports cited documents from September 2010 that showed that the Americans had singled out French diplomats for surveillance while they were working in the United States. The article in Le Monde quoted an internal communications from Susan E. Rice, then the American ambassador to the United Nations, saying that the intelligence on how the French were forming their position on Iran, in particular, was helpful in keeping the United States one step ahead in the negotiations.

docs.snippet: Custom-made from Honduras mahogany, Sueshiro Sano’s beautiful two-wheelers have become objects of veneration and, occasionally, scorn.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sueshiro Sano, a ninth-generation shipwright, makes lightweight, bespoke wooden bicycles in his Tokyo workshop. His bikes, which take three months to assemble and can cost up to $20,000, use Honduras mahogany and are custom built for a 100-percent tailored fit. They’re also impossibly light — a result of Sano’s well-honed boat-building methods — and have become objects of worship, and in some cases, derision, for hipsters and bike experts everywhere. Case in point: at a handmade-bike convention in Denver earlier this year, several incredulous participants accused Sano of using carbon fiber in his designs. (He doesn’t.) But Sano, who built his first boat at 13 and subscribes to the Japanese principle of monozukuri (“making things”), shrugs off such accusations. “For me, it’s about pride,” he says. 011-81-3-5569-6567.

headline.main: Impossibly Light, Totally Sleek Handmade Bikes Built by a Tokyo Shipwright

For waiters, it makes perfect sense — this is among the best service jobs you can find in New York because the tips are so good. (One server I spoke to is an architect who works only part time at his craft, because he makes more money at the restaurant.) But the management earns no tips, and neither does the back-of-house — still, those employees come in and peel potatoes, tenderize steaks, make stocks and generally make the place function. docs.lead_paragraph: Fiona Apple has found a way to let her moods swing even more widely. She has always thrived on a precarious blend of the meticulous and the impulsive, and her current tour, which is billed as a duo with the guitarist, songwriter and producer Blake Mills, opens up new extremes for her to toy with. On Tuesday night at the Beacon Theater, she was skittish and stubborn, baleful and whimsical, giggly between songs and, when she sang, cathartically serious. docs.snippet: The student-members of the Juilliard Orchestra tackled Bartok and Bruckner in a Carnegie Hall concert.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are experts — I’m not one of them — who can identify an orchestra by its sound. During Monday evening’s concert of the Juilliard Orchestra at Carnegie Hall, I found myself wondering what these people would have heard if they had sat blindfolded through this program of works by Bartok and Bruckner, conducted by Alan Gilbert. As powerful waves of rich brass chords rolled out during the last movement of Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7, would they have guessed that the players are students, most in their early 20s? When the sound of the violins intensified with the heat and gleam of molten metal, could they have known that the section was almost entirely made up of women?

headline.main: Student Ensemble’s Sound Belies Its Origin

docs.abstract: And if so, would it discredit conservative health policy ideas as well?
docs.snippet: And if so, would it discredit conservative health policy ideas as well?
docs.lead_paragraph: As a kind of companion piece to my last post on the liberal and conservative visions for health insurance, I strongly recommend reading this post by Mike Konczal, which strikes a note that you can expect to hear sounded more often on the left if the Obamacare rollout continues to go badly. Contra conservatives suggesting that HealthCare.gov represents some kind of discrediting moment for liberalism, Konczal argues that the potential policy problems associated with a nonfunctional web portal really just point to the problems with neoliberalism — a much-debated term of art, but defined for his purposes as the post-1970s idea that social insurance should be “heavy on private provisioning and means-testing,” that it should preserve as much “choice and competition” as possible, and that it should be delivered at the state level or through state-and-federal coordination rather than by the federal government alone.

headline.main: Could Obamacare Discredit Neoliberalism?

docs.lead_paragraph: The Scandinavian artists Michael Elmgreen, 52, and Ingar Dragset, 44, like to place statues of imaginary unhappy inhabitants inside their sculpture installations. For the 2009 Venice Biennale, they floated a simulated corpse of a wealthy, balding art collector face down in a swimming pool. This fall, they turned decrepit galleries at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London into “Tomorrow,” the London apartment of Norman Swann, a mediocre modernist architect who has contracted H.I.V. and run out of inherited money. Along with about 100 objects from the museum’s collection, like an 18th-century Japanese ivory horse figurine and an 1850s plaster fig leaf used to make the museum’s male sculptures less shocking, evidence of Swann’s fictional life is strewn about, including a passport, cigarette butts, unpaid bills, models of unrealized buildings and a biographical script 100 pages long.

docs.abstract: Sausage, cheese and beer? Sure. But look around Wisconsin’s largest city and you’ll also find everything from books to art.
docs.snippet: Sausage, cheese and beer? Sure. But look around Wisconsin’s largest city and you’ll also find everything from books to art.
docs.lead_paragraph: Milwaukee is a city that evolves slowly. Its roots as a blue-collar town — as the German Athens, as Brew City — are still evident in the names of local landmarks (Pabst Theater, Pfister Hotel, Miller Park, where the Milwaukee Brewers play); the neatly demarcated enclaves that still retain strong traces of their ethnic origins; the countless cozy neighborhood taps; and the locals’ love of sausage, cheese and beer, not to mention the array of festivals (German Fest, Irish Fest, Polish Fest) that overtake the lakefront every summer. Yet this city — Wisconsin’s largest, population 600,000 — is hardly a backward-looking place. Following a few decades of diminishing population, numbers have risen slightly in the years since the 2010 census, much of the increase due to young people moving into a few revived downtown neighborhoods like Walker’s Point and the southerly, suddenly hip Bay View, with its bars and galleries. The result is a city that possesses a renewed vitality while still holding on to an Old World character.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Milwaukee

docs.lead_paragraph: That first time I walked through the grassy dunes of Point Reyes National Seashore, back in 1997, it felt familiar. On this stretch of California sand, I’d found the West Coast doppelgänger of Gay Head, on the southwestern point of Martha’s Vineyard, from where I’d recently moved. Though it was summer, I was wearing a fleece, and the sandstone cliffs of Limantour Beach were shrouded in fog. But the echoes of the Vineyard in Point Reyes were immediately clear: a rugged, relatively remote refuge with salty air, fresh fish and a strong sense of place.

docs.lead_paragraph: If you like old clocks — and who doesn’t like old clocks? — there’s one you must see in the International Fine Art & Antique Dealers Show at the Park Avenue Armory. Displayed by Richard Redding Antiques, one of the show’s 67 vendors, it’s called “The Hartmann Exhibition Clock,” and it’s spectacular. A gleaming, complicated assemblage of gilt bronze, it has a neo-classical base from which columns resembling minarets made of basket-woven metal bands rise. These flank a roughly pyramidal tower of eight different clocks with enameled faces keeping time according to as many different systems. At the summit a little figure of Victory blows a trumpet. It also has a variety of automata, including small silver rods whose revolutions suggest streams of falling water.

headline.main: Part Ostentatious, Part Intimate

docs.lead_paragraph: If you haven’t quite wrapped your head around the concept of 3-D printing, or haven’t yet had a digital scanner wrap itself around you, now you can do both in “Out of Hand: Materializing the Postdigital,” at the Museum of Arts and Design. docs.snippet: “The Square,” Jehane Noujaim’s new documentary, makes the Egyptian uprising and the political fallout of this summer feel close and personal.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the language of politics, “the people” is a great abstraction, an idea that can be invoked to justify noble projects and terrible crimes. “The Square,” Jehane Noujaim’s stunning new documentary, is partly about the contested status of the Egyptian people between the winter of 2011, when crowds of protesters gathered in Tahrir Square to demand the removal of President Hosni Mubarak, and the summer of 2013, when the army ousted his successor, Mohamed Morsi, and began a violent campaign against his followers in the Muslim Brotherhood. Mr. Morsi, the military and the demonstrators — and, for that matter, Mr. Mubarak himself — all claimed to be true agents and loyal servants of the popular will.

headline.main: Brave Optimism of Tahrir Square Meets Other Fierce Forces

docs.snippet: The shell of a forsaken ship has become a battleground in a struggle that could shape the future of the South China Sea and, to some extent, the rest of the world.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a remote corner of the South China Sea, 105 nautical miles from the Philippines, lies a submerged reef that the Filipinos call Ayungin. There’s little to commend the spot, apart from its plentiful fish and safe harbor. In most ways it resembles the hundreds of other desolate reefs, islands, rock clusters and cays that collectively are called the Spratly Islands. But Ayungin is different. It sits on the southwestern edge of Reed Bank, an area rumored to contain vast reserves of oil and natural gas. And its shallows are home to a World War II-era ship called the Sierra Madre, which the Philippine government ran aground on the reef in 1999 and has since maintained as a kind of post-apocalyptic military garrison, manned by eight Filipino troops struggling to survive extreme mental and physical desolation. Of all places, the scorched shell of the Sierra Madre has become an unlikely battleground in a geopolitical struggle that will shape the future of the South China Sea and, to some extent, the rest of the world.

docs.snippet: The case, one of the most notorious recent child-abduction cases in Europe, was formally closed in 2008.
docs.lead_paragraph: Portuguese prosecutors on Thursday reopened an investigation into the disappearance of Madeleine McCann from her British parents’ hotel room six years ago, when she was 3. The case, one of the most notorious recent child-abduction cases in Europe, was formally closed in 2008. But after a campaign by the girl’s parents, Kate and Gerry McCann, British and Portuguese investigators began reviewing the evidence two years ago and independently uncovered new leads. In July, British officials opened a formal investigation, and now Portugal has followed suit. Portuguese investigators did not specify what the new leads were, but according to the police in London they are separate from the ones being followed in Britain. Teams from both countries met a week ago to compare notes and to brief the McCanns on the progress. Madeleine disappeared on May 3, 2007, from an apartment in a resort in Praia da Luz, Portugal, while her parents were having dinner at a nearby restaurant.

headline.main: Portugal: Investigators Reopen Case of Missing British Child

docs.abstract: The jeweler, actor and man-about-town will stock unique items from artisans in his new boutique, opening in November, which takes inspiration from ancient trade routes.
docs.snippet: The jeweler, actor and man-about-town will stock unique items from artisans in his new boutique, opening in November, which takes inspiration from ancient trade routes.
docs.lead_paragraph: Think of Waris Ahluwalia, the jeweler, actor and man-about-every-town, as a modern-day Marco Polo, bringing back implements of leisure from foreign ports of call: Morocco, Bali, India, Sweden, Lebanon. Next month, he opens his House of Waris Rare shop inside the library of Venice’s lavish Gritti Palace hotel. “I’m not just interested in well-designed trophies,” he says. “Whatever we stock should serve an actual purpose.” He steers away from comparisons to Paris’s Deyrolle or any upscale curiosity boutique, talking instead about revisiting ancient trade routes. In some ways this project is the culmination of a three-year expedition he began with the Luxury Collection, which owns the hotel and commissioned Ahluwalia as its global explorer. Everything sold at the shop — engraved tumblers hand-blown in Murano, vintage Fortuny fabrics fashioned into stuffed animals — is the type of affectionate object one might imagine, say, Ernest Hemingway gifting his mistress. Ahluwalia has stocked the shop with unique goods from artisans both emerging and established, including his own fine jewelry. “You can’t just ogle and awe,” he says about these collectibles. “You must engage as a patron. It’s not just the items that are unique — so too are the people who make them.”

headline.main: In Store | Waris Ahluwalia Opens an Old-World Market in Venice

docs.abstract: How a lawsuit sent America’s inventors to work.
docs.snippet: How a lawsuit sent America’s inventors to work.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the late 1970s, when you ordered coffee to go, you usually had to tear a hole in the plastic lid if you wanted to drink through it. This maneuver was so awkward that you risked burning your hand. So in the 1980s, a number of food-packaging engineers tried to fix the problem. William and Kenneth Dart, of the Dart Container Corporation, created one of the first of a new breed of coffee-cup lids, filing a patent in 1981 for a plastic disc with a press-down tab that acted like a valve. The inventors called this feature a “lip-engaging buttress”; you pushed on it with your upper lip to release a gulp of coffee. Once you finished drinking, the tab snapped back into place to prevent spills. (Kenneth Dart, who made a fortune in this and other business ventures, later renounced his citizenship and moved to Belize, where he was exempt from U.S. taxes.)

headline.main: Who Made That Coffee Lid?

docs.lead_paragraph: The Golden Rule (usually defined as “One should treat others as one would like to be treated”) is attractive to people as a guiding principle for ethical conduct. However I feel that in our diverse, modern world, it is less than ideal. By assuming other people should be treated the way I want to be treated, it imposes my preferences and values on those around me. Wouldn’t a better rule be “One should treat others as they want to be treated”? GARRETT FRY, MONROVIA, CALIF.

Stanton, a 29-year-old Georgia native, started photographing strangers in 2010 after finding his way to New York from Chicago, where he had recently lost his job as a bond trader. “My mom basically thought this was my glorified way of not working,” he told ABC’s “Nightline” last month. “Like, oh, Brandon’s in New York taking pictures of people on the street and putting them on Facebook, you know what I mean?” That description isn’t far off the mark, actually. But it misses the primal voyeuristic appeal of Stanton’s blog, which only increased after he started interviewing his subjects and including short quotations or anecdotes with their portraits. (“Q. docs.snippet: A biography of the British wayfarer, soldier and travel writer Patrick Leigh Fermor.
docs.lead_paragraph: Surprise is the keynote of the best travel writing. The travel writer should be knowledgeable but not an expert, open in mind and body to the unforeseen twists of serendipity. But what we most require from travel writing, as opposed to mere guidebooks, is that elusive quality Nick Carraway defined as “romantic readiness.” Few 20th-century figures combined these traits in a more appealing package than the English writer Patrick Leigh Fermor, Paddy to his many friends, who died in 2011 at the age of 96. One of these was Diana Cooper, a famous beauty who turned up in the fiction of Evelyn Waugh. Now Artemis Cooper, her granddaughter, has written an affectionately intimate, informative and forgiving biography of Diana’s complicated friend.

docs.abstract: Sara Wheeler follows six 19th-century women who left England and reinvented themselves in the United States.
docs.snippet: Sara Wheeler follows six 19th-century women who left England and reinvented themselves in the United States.
docs.lead_paragraph: Just give in — I finally did — to the rough-edged charms of Sara Wheeler’s latest hybrid of historical narrative and travelogue. Never mind that Wheeler, a British author whose previous book, “Terra Incognita,” chronicled her adventures in Antarctica, commits the same sin as at least two of the six women writers she profiles: Fanny Trollope, whose withering account of life along the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers, “Domestic Manners of the Americans,” infuriated American readers; and Fanny Kemble Butler, whose reflexively judgmental “Journal of a Residence in America” provoked a breach with her American husband. Wheeler seems not to have calculated the effects of her own gratuitous insults, whether aimed at the “agreeable Fatty­towns” of the Midwest or the “crap of contemporary America” she encounters at a once-grand seaside resort community in Massachusetts. Even her praise can be faintly damning: “On the whole Americans are a friendly, polite lot.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Metafiction is often more fun to write than it is to read. Everything on the page is the result of a series of strenuous choices, none inevitable, and reminding the reader just who made these choices (whether conscious or not) can be amusing, aesthetically useful and a great relief from the constraints of the traditional conventions of fiction. But intelligent readers may not need reminding, may even take it as an insult. They know who the puppets are and who the puppeteer. They have sought out fiction for a reason: quite often they simply wish the puppeteer would shut up, back away and get on with the storytelling.

docs.lead_paragraph: We spotted the craftsman first, alone in his workshop, a cubby barely larger than a closet. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of such stalls in the medina in Fez, an ancient city within a city of winding paths and centuries-old artisanship, where vendors tout their leather and oils on every corner. But this stall stood out. It was nearly bare, not crammed as most of the others were with doodads to be fussed and negotiated over. A few tools hung on the wall, alongside the red Moroccan flag with its green pentagram, and some old photos of the craftsman, now white-haired and wearing a traditional long robe.

docs.lead_paragraph: Just before 9 p.m. on a recent Thursday in London, five guided tour groups, about 150 people in all, converged on a nondescript courtyard on the eastern edge of the central financial district. Some tour guides wore 19th-century top hats and long, dark cloaks. Others grasped photographs of mortuary corpses. And each guide jostled for the best spot: near the tiny flower bed in the far corner where, in 1888, Jack the Ripper murdered a prostitute named Catherine Eddowes — slitting her throat, slashing her face, pulling out her innards and walking off with her uterus.

headline.main: Competing to Tell Jack the Ripper’s Story

docs.lead_paragraph: SAN FRANCISCO — Although it would be hard to tell from the volume of his work, David Hockney, now 76, has had a rough year. Last October, this celebrated British artist had a stroke, which left him unable to complete his sentences for a time. In March, one of his studio assistants in East Yorkshire, part of a tight-knit circle of aides, collaborators and former lovers, died in Mr. Hockney’s home after drinking drain cleaner on the heels of a drug binge. docs.lead_paragraph: In 1957, in an exchange that passed quickly into performance lore, the critic Louis Horst published a blank column in response to “Duet,” a Paul Taylor dance comprising stillness and set to John Cage’s “4’33.” I thought with longing of Horst’s gorgeous expanse of silence Thursday night at the Brooklyn Academy of Music Harvey Theater, during “Hans was Heiri” by the Swiss duo Zimmermann & de Perrot — not because this physical theater work is minimalist, but for the opposite reason. Blankness seemed the only possible antidote to this relentlessly busy and manic spectacle; it was like the desire to slip into a hermetically sealed, fragrance-free chamber after shopping at Sephora.

docs.abstract: Advisers to the Food and Drug Administration unanimously voted in favor of a hepatitis C drug from Gilead Sciences.
docs.snippet: Advisers to the Food and Drug Administration unanimously voted in favor of a hepatitis C drug from Gilead Sciences.
docs.lead_paragraph: Advisers to the Food and Drug Administration unanimously voted in favor of a hepatitis C drug from Gilead Sciences. All 15 members of the agency’s panel of virus experts voted to recommend approval of Gilead’s pill, sofosbuvir, to treat several forms of the disease, which afflicts more than three million people in the United States. The agency is not required to adhere to the group’s advice, though it often does. Current treatments can take up to a year of therapy and cure only about three out of four patients. Gilead’s daily pill can cure up to 90 percent of patients infected with the most common form of the virus in just 12 weeks. Gilead, based in Foster City, Calif., is one of a half-dozen companies racing to develop more effective treatments for hepatitis C. The agency is expected to make a decision on the drug by Dec. 8.

This is by no means the best movie of the year, but it may be the most movie you can get for the price of a single ticket.” Its six sections also star Doona Bae, Jim Broadbent, Keith David, Hugh Grant, Susan Sarandon, Jim Sturgess, Hugo Weaving and Ben Whishaw. “Together the filmmakers try so hard to give you everything — the secrets of the universe and the human heart; action, laughs and romance; tragedy and mystery — that you may wind up feeling both grateful and disappointed.”

docs.abstract: Gem lovers will have plenty to enjoy next month, with exhibits devoted to the legendary designers JAR and Alexandre Reza, and a book devoted to 400 years of Indian jewelry.
docs.snippet: Gem lovers will have plenty to enjoy next month, with exhibits devoted to the legendary designers JAR and Alexandre Reza, and a book devoted to 400 years of Indian jewelry.
docs.lead_paragraph: Diamonds may be a girl’s best friend, but next month is all about men designing and collecting some of the world’s greatest gems. The Paris-based Joel Arthur Rosenthal, known professionally as JAR — an acronym synonymous for more than 35 years with ne plus ultra jewels fashioned into spirals, flowers and butterflies — will unveil his first American retrospective, “Jewels by JAR,” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Meanwhile, Sotheby’s will showcase the rarest pieces made by the retired Alexandre Reza, in addition to designs by his son Olivier, with an exhibition, “The Extraordinary Jewelry of Alexandre Reza.” Finally, Sheikh Hamad bin Abdullah Al Thani of Qatar boasts an unparalleled private collection of Indian jewels spanning the past 400 years — from handcrafted jade daggers of the Mughal courts to emerald turban ornaments favored by 19th-century maharajahs — which have been bound into a beautiful tome.

headline.main: By Design | High Season for High Jewels

docs.lead_paragraph: It is one of the fashion industry’s more epic feats of longevity that Giorgio Armani is breezily approaching his fifth decade of design under his namesake label. But you don’t create a multibillion dollar empire that spans clothes, home décor, hotels, restaurants and even the silver screen without raising a few eyebrows. After all, this is the man responsible for shifting the boundaries of permissible images of male eroticism with Richard Gere’s wardrobe in “American Gigolo,” and for helping to define the prowess of grab-and-greed 1980s power-suit dressing for women — which, by extension, has become the uniform of choice for Hollywood honchos, Wall Street bigwigs and red-carpet mainstays to this day. But as is the Armani M.O., all epoch-making moments appear as effortless as his signature bronzed physique and glowing white smile.

headline.main: Giorgio Armani’s Dolce Vita

docs.abstract: This weekend, 26-year-old Sebastian Vettel became the third and youngest Formula One driver to win four consecutive championship titles.
docs.snippet: This weekend, 26-year-old Sebastian Vettel became the third and youngest Formula One driver to win four consecutive championship titles.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sebastian Vettel, the Red Bull Infiniti driver, clinched his fourth consecutive Formula One championship with a victory Sunday in the Indian Grand Prix at the Buddh International Circuit near New Delhi. docs.lead_paragraph: On Saturday night, the downtown set gathered in a photo studio in Chelsea to celebrate the introduction of a new “literary and erotic magazine” called Adult. Stepping off of the quiet street and into the large, vaulted space — barely decorated but stocked with an abundance of beer and bubbly, a few bowls filled with nostalgic Halloween candy like Dubble Bubble and standard issue lollipops, a couple of penis-shaped piñatas hanging next to a stage (where Kelela and Lauren Devine performed later in the night), and old-school pornography, projected onto a large white wall for the party’s duration — was like discovering a clandestine and slightly naughty affair, which is the same experience the founding editor Sarah Nicole Prickett wants you to have when opening her inaugural issue. “I wanted Adult to feel like a secret,” she said about the quarterly magazine, which will hit select newsstands, including Marc Jacobs’s bookstore, BookMarc, and the Museum of Modern Art, in mid-November. Despite the “Not for sale to minors” disclaimer on its cover, Prickett isn’t shy about hoping the young and curious find it, even if they have to steal it. “I want to go on the record as being very pro-minors,” she said. “I love teen girls. I wish I could have been one — I was awful at it. The best I can hope for is the feeling I had as a teen, which is that I couldn’t wait to get older. I want people to feel like that until they’re 70.”

headline.main: Bookshelf | An Erotic Magazine for Voyeurs and Literati Alike

docs.abstract: Iran said that it would oppose attempts by Azerbaijan to officially register polo with the United Nations as a purely indigenous sport, arguing that polo is an international game.
docs.snippet: Iran said that it would oppose attempts by Azerbaijan to officially register polo with the United Nations as a purely indigenous sport, arguing that polo is an international game.
docs.lead_paragraph: Iran said Monday that it would oppose attempts by Azerbaijan to officially register polo with the United Nations as a purely indigenous sport, arguing that polo is an international game and Azerbaijan has no right to claim that it originated there. The official Islamic Republic News Agency quoted Mohammad-Ali Najafi, the head of Iran’s Cultural Heritage, Handicrafts and Tourism Organization, as saying in a letter to Unesco that “Iran strongly requests the rejection” of Azerbaijan’s application to register polo — which both nations call chogan — as an entry on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity list. Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan and India are among the countries that also have a claim on the game, the world’s oldest known competitive team sport, in which players on horseback use mallets to swat a ball through the opposing side’s goal posts. Unesco — the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization — will decide on Azerbaijan’s application during a meeting of its Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage to be held in Baku, Azerbaijan, Dec. 2-7.

headline.main: Iran: Dispute with Azerbaijan Over Polo

docs.abstract: Is it a coincidence when your iPhone stops working just as the new models come out?
docs.snippet: Is it a coincidence when your iPhone stops working just as the new models come out?
docs.lead_paragraph: At first, I thought it was my imagination. Around the time the iPhone 5S and 5C were released, in September, I noticed that my sad old iPhone 4 was becoming a lot more sluggish. The battery was starting to run down much faster, too. But the same thing seemed to be happening to a lot of people who, like me, swear by their Apple products. When I called tech analysts, they said that the new operating system (iOS 7) being pushed out to existing users was making older models unbearably slow. Apple phone batteries, which have a finite number of charges in them to begin with, were drained by the new software. So I could pay Apple $79 to replace the battery, or perhaps spend 20 bucks more for an iPhone 5C. It seemed like Apple was sending me a not-so-subtle message to upgrade.

headline.main: Cracking the Apple Trap

docs.lead_paragraph: IN 1893, Charles Eliot, president of Harvard, introduced to the National Education Association a novel concept: the credit hour. Roughly equivalent to one hour of lecture time a week for a 12- to 14-week semester, it became the basic unit of a college education, and the standard measure for transferring work between institutions. To be accredited, universities have had to base curriculums on credit hours and years of study. The seat-time system — one based on the hours spent in the classroom — is further reinforced by Title IV student aid: to receive need-based Pell grants or federal loans, students have had to carry a certain load of credits each semester.

A softly fruity wine like a well-balanced zinfandel or Russian River Valley pinot noir may go surprisingly well, cushioning the jagged flavors and complementing the harmony of spices, provided they are not extravagantly alcoholic and are served slightly cool. As a sherry fanatic, I think oloroso, even with its high level of alcohol, around 20 percent, would pair beautifully. You might also try sweet wines, like a demi-sec Vouvray or an auslese riesling from the Mosel. These wines will be even better with 10 or 15 years of age.

headline.main: For Red-Cooked Beef, a Softly Fruity Wine
headline.print_headline: And to Drink...

docs.snippet: Made with a blend of natural oils, the new body serum from the New York skin care line Kahina Giving Beauty has a scent that's intended to transport its wearer straight to Fez.
docs.lead_paragraph: Pure argan oil, responsibly sourced from Morocco, is the key ingredient in all of the products made by the New York organic skin care line Kahina Giving Beauty, founded five years ago by Katharine L’Heureux. The brand’s signature product, a bottle of 100 percent organic argan oil, works as well on the face and body as it does on hair, soothing dryness and replenishing moisture. But for Kahina’s first body serum, L’Heureux combined a lightweight argan oil base with 16 other oils, from watermelon and coconut to cumin and clove, to “create this more luxurious spreadable texture,” she said. It’s also the brand’s first scented product. The aroma is called Fez. Putting it on is a warm, sensory experience meant to transport the wearer to the Moroccan city, one of L’Heureux’s favorite places. “I wanted something evocative of that multilayered city that combines spirituality with all the scents of the spice market and the souk and the floral notes that happen in the spring, when the orange flower blossoms are just spilling through the streets,” L’Heureux explained. “I’ve never personally been a big scent person, but I love the idea of evoking places.” She plans to introduce additional products with the same spicy scent. $98; givingbeauty.com.

headline.main: Morocco in a Bottle

Scully, 56, is slightly taller than average and has tousled graying hair, an athletic build and a lopsided smile. He typically projects a combination of confidence and bemusement, but on this rainy September afternoon, he was frenzied. Scully was scheduled to deliver the keynote address at an event hosted by the Potomac Research Group, a Beltway firm that advises large investors on government policy (tag line: “Washington to Wall Street”). Today’s discussion centered on the most significant change in decades to the nation’s health care policy, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, a.k.a. Obamacare. As Scully walked to the front of the room, some 50 managers from hedge funds, mutual funds and private equity firms tucked into the round tables. Others gathered in the hallway. A hush of anticipation hung in the air.

docs.lead_paragraph: JERUSALEM — The Pew Research Center released a comprehensive and nuanced study on Oct. 1 about the character of the American Jewish community. The reaction here was typical Israeli apprehension about Jews’ place in the world, mixed with a general sense of confusion over how to interpret the results. Most discussions focused on two aspects: The high percentage of interfaith marriages and the vast support among American Jews for Israel.Fifty-eight percent of Jews who married between 2005 and 2013 have a non-Jewish spouse. Mixed marriages inevitably lead to the assimilation of Jews into American culture, and tap long-standing Israeli fears over the future of the Jewish people. To some Israelis given to these worries, assimilation is tantamount to accepting annihilation.

headline.main: Israel Gets a Mixed Message on American Jews

docs.abstract: The many levels of meaning in Eastman Johnson’s great emancipation work, “The Lord Is My Shepherd.”
docs.snippet: The many levels of meaning in Eastman Johnson’s great emancipation work, “The Lord Is My Shepherd.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Sometime in the early fall of 1863, the artist Eastman Johnson composed a small work that he titled “The Lord Is My Shepherd.” At first glance, the image seems to posit the gentle nature of a formerly enslaved man reading the Psalms as a model of emerging humanity and citizenship. Johnson’s warm, sepia-toned brushwork provides little detail in the architecture of the setting. The young black man sits on a folding stool with a canvas seat, absorbed in the book he holds in his powerful hand; a dark blue coat lined in scarlet is draped over the back of the chair, possibly hinting that he has served in the Union Army. Wide wooden planks mark the transition from hearth to floorboards, sketching out a crude dwelling.

headline.main: Painting Freedom
